concepts.name: debounce vs sample for rate-limiting flows
Kotlin `internal` visibility as a module boundary

questions.prompt: A GPS flow emits a location every 50 ms while the user drives, and the map should redraw at most twice a second for as long as the car keeps moving. Which operator fits?

choices.text: `debounce(500)`, which emits the newest value once every 500 ms
`distinctUntilChanged()`, which drops values that arrive too fast
`sample(500)`, which emits the latest value of each 500 ms window
`conflate()`, which keeps just one location for every 500 ms period

questions.explanation: `sample` emits the latest value of each sampling period, so a steady 50 ms stream becomes one value every 500 ms. `debounce` drops every value that is followed by a newer one within the timeout, so it emits nothing at all while values keep arriving faster than every 500 ms: the map would freeze until the car stopped. `conflate` has no time window; it just skips values the collector is too slow for.

sources.title: sample
sources.claim: sample returns a flow that emits only the latest value emitted by the original flow during each sampling period.

sources.title: debounce
sources.claim: debounce filters out values followed by newer values within the timeout, and emits nothing as long as the original flow emits faster than every timeoutMillis.

questions.prompt: Your SDK, shipped as an AAR, creates some of its classes by reflection. Apps that use it crash once they turn on R8. Where should the SDK's keep rules go?

choices.text: In `consumerProguardFiles`, which are packaged into the AAR for apps
In the library's `proguardFiles`, which R8 applies when apps build
In the README, asking apps to add `-dontobfuscate` to their own rules
Nowhere: R8 leaves AAR code untouched unless the app opts in to it

questions.explanation: Rules in `consumerProguardFiles` are bundled into the AAR and applied automatically when an app that depends on the library is optimized, so they should keep whatever the library reaches by reflection. `proguardFiles` only apply while the library itself is built. `-dontobfuscate` is a global option libraries shouldn't push on apps, and it wouldn't stop R8 removing the unreferenced classes anyway.

sources.title: Optimization for library authors
sources.claim: consumerProguardFiles are packaged into the library (AAR or JAR) and applied when an app that consumes it is optimized, and must keep what the library reflects on; proguardFiles are used only at library build time; libraries shouldn't use global rules such as -dontobfuscate.

questions.prompt: A teammate says moving a feature into its own Gradle module improves encapsulation. Explain how Kotlin's `internal` works, why it hides more after the split, and one exception to keep in mind.

model_answer.summary: `internal` means visible within one Kotlin module, such as a Gradle source set, so after the split everything except the feature's public interface can be made `internal` or `private` and other modules can't use it.
key_points: An `internal` declaration is visible only inside the same module: a set of Kotlin files compiled together, such as a Gradle source set
In one big app module, `internal` hides nothing from other features, because they are all in the same module
After the split, the feature can mark everything except its public interface `internal` or `private`, so other modules can't depend on its internals
The `test` source set can still see the `internal` declarations of `main`, so tests can reach internals

questions.explanation: Gradle modules give `internal` its teeth. Android's modularization guide lists this as strict visibility control: other parts of the code know only the small public API, which keeps coupling low. A common slip is to think `internal` is like Java package-private; it is about the compilation unit, not the package.

sources.title: Visibility modifiers
sources.claim: internal means visible within the same module, a set of Kotlin files compiled together such as a Gradle source set, except that the test source set can access internal declarations of main.

sources.title: Guide to Android app modularization
sources.claim: Modules give strict visibility control: you can mark everything but your public interface as internal or private to prevent it being used outside the module.

questions.prompt:
What does this flow emit?

```kotlin
flow {
  emit(1); delay(90); emit(2); delay(90); emit(3)
  delay(1010); emit(4); delay(1010); emit(5)
}.debounce(1000)
```
questions.explanation: `debounce(1000)` drops a value if a newer one arrives within 1000 ms. `1` and `2` are each followed by another value 90 ms later, so they are dropped; `3` and `4` are followed by more than 1000 ms of quiet, so they pass. `5` is the last value, and debounce always emits the latest value when the flow completes.

sources.title: debounce
sources.claim: debounce filters out values followed by newer values within the timeout and always emits the latest value; the documented example with emits 1, 2, 3 (90 ms apart), 4 and 5 (1010 ms apart) and debounce(1000) produces 3, 4, 5.

questions.prompt: Which of these should a library's consumer keep rules file not contain?

choices.text: `-keep` rules for the classes the library creates by reflection
Rules for the methods its JNI code calls back into by their name
Rules that keep only the members its JSON parser reads reflectively

questions.explanation: Consumer rules are merged into every app that uses the library, so they should be narrow: keep what the library reaches by reflection or JNI, and nothing more. Global options such as `-dontobfuscate`, `-repackageclasses` or `-allowaccessmodification` change how the whole app is optimized, and the library guidance says not to ship them; nor should libraries ship broad package-wide `-keep` rules.

sources.title: Optimization for library authors
sources.claim: Consumer keep rules should keep what the library reflects on or calls through JNI; libraries shouldn't include broad package-wide keep rules or global options such as -dontobfuscate, -allowaccessmodification or -repackageclasses.

questions.prompt: `:feature:cart` declares `internal class CartPricer`. Which code can use `CartPricer`?

choices.text: Any module that depends on `:feature:cart` through `implementation` or `api`
Code in `:feature:cart`'s main and test source sets, and no other module
Only code in the same Kotlin package, like Java's package-private
Any Kotlin code in the app, since `internal` hides it only from Java

questions.explanation: In Kotlin, `internal` means visible inside the same module, a set of files compiled together such as a Gradle source set, and a `test` source set can also see `main`'s internals. Depending on the module doesn't grant access, and `internal` is not tied to packages the way Java's package-private is.

sources.title: Visibility modifiers
sources.claim: internal declarations are visible everywhere in the same module (such as a Gradle source set), and the test source set can access the internal declarations of main.
